narrative:
The model estimates your chance of failing at 25%. That is not a certainty, but it means roughly one in four students with a similar profile would not pass, and the school treats that risk as high enough to require remedial courses as a safeguard.

The strongest influences in your prediction actually worked in your favor. The most important was your past class failures: you have none, matching the passer average, which strongly pushed toward passing. Second was your goal to continue to higher education: you said yes, as did every passer in the comparison group, so this also reduced your risk. Third was family size: you are in a small family of three or fewer. This was less common among passers—about 35% versus 66% in larger families—but it still nudged your prediction toward passing.

So the top signals are protective. The model still flags risk because other, weaker factors add up. You study under two hours a week, while most passers study two to five hours. You also go out often and report very high weekend alcohol use, both less common among passers. To improve your position, raise your weekly study time, reduce weekend drinking and nights out, and ask your family for academic support rather than handling coursework alone.
